slides.title: constexpr vs const
slides.prompt: What is the key difference between const and constexpr variables?
options: constexpr requires initialization with a compile-time constant; const can be initialized with runtime values
const variables are evaluated at compile time; constexpr at runtime
constexpr variables cannot be primitive data types
const applies only to functions, while constexpr applies to variables
slides.correctAnswer: constexpr requires initialization with a compile-time constant; const can be initialized with runtime values

slides.title: constexpr Function Rule

slides.title: Runtime Execution of constexpr Functions
slides.prompt: Can a constexpr function be invoked with non-constexpr runtime arguments?
options: Yes, and in that case it executes at runtime like a normal function
No, calling it with non-const arguments causes a compile error
Yes, but it converts runtime values to static constants
No, constexpr functions are deleted from runtime binaries
slides.correctAnswer: Yes, and in that case it executes at runtime like a normal function

slides.title: C++14 Relaxation of constexpr Functions
slides.prompt: Which feature was added to constexpr functions in C++14?
options: Support for local variable declarations, loops, and multiple return statements
Support for dynamic stack allocation using new
Permission to throw unhandled runtime exceptions
slides.correctAnswer: Support for local variable declarations, loops, and multiple return statements

slides.title: Literal Types Requirement
slides.prompt: What is a requirement for a custom class to be used as a constexpr variable type?

It must not contain any member functions
It must be declared inside an anonymous namespace
